en: 1. First Section of the *Vigrahavyāvartanī-kārikā*, Part One.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Wei Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Vimokṣasena together with Gautama Ratnākara.
Question: A verse says:
"If all things lack intrinsic nature, then speech itself is all things."
Language itself has no intrinsic nature; how could it negate the nature of others?
If language possessed an intrinsic nature, the thesis previously established would be undermined.
Such being the case, there is a fault, and you ought to state a superior reason.
If you claim that it is like the sound "do not," this meaning is not so;
for while a sound can obstruct another sound, how could the absence of sound obstruct anything?
Your claim that there is a negation of what is to be negated is likewise not so;
for if the characteristics of your own thesis are thus self-subverting, they do not belong to me.
If that which appears were truly existent, you might be able to turn back [from it].
That which appears is likewise non-existent; how then can it be grasped or turned away?
One speaks of the four means of valid cognition—direct perception, inference, scripture, and analogy.
Direct perception is established by that [non-existence], as is scripture, and analogy is also able to establish it.
The wise know how to teach the Dharma; they know that wholesome dharmas possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Worldly people likewise recognize that things have an essence, and other phenomena are also like this.
That dharmas arise from their own intrinsic nature is what has been taught by the Noble Ones.
In this way, that which does not emerge has no emergent intrinsic nature.
If all phenomena lack an intrinsic nature, then lacking an intrinsic nature, they cannot be designated by names.
If there is an intrinsic nature, then there is a name; but how can that which is merely a name be called a "name"?
If a name existed apart from the phenomena, and yet that name did not exist within those very phenomena—
should one say that a name exists apart from the phenomena, such a person may be challenged.
If phenomena possessed an intrinsic nature, it would be possible to negate all phenomena.
If all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, what exactly is there to be negated?
Just as when a jar or clay exists, one can negate the jar or the clay;
one negates upon seeing an existing thing, but one does not negate when seeing nothing at all.
If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, what could language possibly negate?
If negation were possible without an object to be negated, then negation would also be established even without words.
It is like a foolish person who falsely perceives a mirage as water.
If you negate false apprehension, the principle applies equally to that matter as well.
Apprehended object, apprehending subject, and the act of apprehension;
negated object, negating subject, and the act of negation—these six categories of meaning are all existent phenomena.
If there is neither the grasped nor the object of grasping, and likewise no grasper,
then there is neither the negated nor the object of negation, and likewise no negator.
If there is neither the negated nor the object of negation, and likewise no negator, [then all things are empty].
Then all phenomena would be established, and their intrinsic nature would also be established;
yet your reason would not be established—for how can that which lacks an intrinsic nature serve as a reason?
If a phenomenon has no cause, how can it be said to be established?
If you establish [your position] without a reason, then the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is overturned;
yet if I also establish [mine] without a reason, then all phenomena possess intrinsic nature.
If there were a reason but no intrinsic nature, this meaning would be inconsistent.
If worldly phenomena lack intrinsic nature, one cannot say they exist.
If the prior negation and the subsequent object of negation were thus incompatible,
or if the subsequent negation and the [prior] coexisted, then one would know them to have intrinsic nature.
"If my words were separate from the phenomena produced by the harmony of causes and conditions,
then the meaning of emptiness would be established, and all dharmas would lack intrinsic nature.
Since the phenomena of causes and conditions are empty, I now explain this meaning."
Who possesses causes and conditions?
Those causes and conditions lack intrinsic substance.
A conjured person toward another conjured person; an illusory person toward another illusory person.
In this way, the negation and that which is negated are of the same nature.
Since words lack intrinsic nature, that which is expressed likewise lacks intrinsic nature.
Thus, I am without fault and need not state a superior reason.
As for your mention of the sound "do not," this is not my analogy;
it is not by means of this sound that I am able to negate that sound.
Just as if some man were to falsely perceive the body of a conjured woman and give rise to a mind of desire, so too is this meaning.
It is not the case that the same [logical] proof applies here, because there is no cause within an echo.
I rely upon conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) And therefore speak in this way.
If one does not rely upon conventional truth, One cannot realize ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
If one does not realize ultimate truth, One cannot attain the realization of nirvāṇa.
If my own school held that [the self] exists, then I would be at fault;
since my school holds that there is no such thing, I am not subject to this fault.
If I were to adopt [the existence of the self] and then turn back from it, I would necessarily have to employ [pramāṇas] such as direct perception.
If [the means of knowledge] were grasped through another [means], there would be an infinite regress; if it were not so, what would be the fault?
If a means of knowledge were established by a means of knowledge, that [second] one must in turn be established by a means of knowledge.
Where, then, do you say that a means of knowledge could be established?
If a means of valid cognition were established apart from other means of valid cognition, your argument would fail;
such being the case, there is a fault, and you ought to state a superior reason.
It is like fire: because it is luminous, it can illuminate both itself and others.
That means of knowledge is likewise established for both oneself and others.
Your statement contains a fallacy; fire does not illuminate itself, because that is inconsistent, just as one sees a jar in the dark.
Furthermore, if you say that fire can illuminate both itself and others,
just as fire can burn others, why does it not burn itself?
Furthermore, if you say that fire can illuminate both itself and others...
Darkness should also be understood in this way: it obscures both itself and others.
Since there is no darkness within fire, where could self and other abide?
If that darkness can destroy light, how could fire possess light?
Thus, when fire arises, it is able to illuminate at the very moment of its arising;
yet for fire to reach darkness at that same moment is logically inconsistent.
If fire were able to destroy darkness without reaching it, [it would follow that it could destroy all darkness everywhere].
If fire were to abide here, it should destroy all darkness.
If a means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) could establish itself independently, without depending on the object of cognition (*prameya*) for its establishment,
then that means of cognition would be self-established and would not depend on anything else for its establishment.
If your means of cognition were established without depending on the object of cognition,
then there would be no person who employs a means of cognition to cognize all phenomena.
If the object of cognition were established by depending on the means of cognition, [the means of cognition would likewise depend on the object].
If this [object] were established by the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would be established only after depending upon that means of cognition.
If an object were established without depending on a means of cognition, then it would not depend on a means of cognition;
why then do you claim that it is established by a means of cognition?
What is established by that means of valid cognition?
If you claim that the means of valid cognition is established by that [object], and that which is to be cognized is established in dependence upon it,
then the means of valid cognition and the object of cognition would be thus inseparable.
If the means of cognition establishes the object of cognition, or if the object of cognition establishes the means of cognition—
if you hold such a view, both are unestablished.
It is not that the means of cognition can establish the object of cognition, nor that the object of cognition can establish the means of cognition.
If this were the case, how could they establish one another?
How could the object of cognition establish the means of cognition, and the means of cognition establish the object of cognition?
If this were the case, how could they establish one another?
Does the father give birth to the son,
or does the son give birth to the father?
Which of these is the progenitor?
What is that which is produced? What is the father?
And what is the son?
Regarding these two types you have described, the relationship between father and son is open to doubt.
A valid cognition cannot be established by itself; it is not established by both self and other;
it is not established by another cognition; nor is it established without causes and conditions.
If, as the Dharma Master says, wholesome dharmas possess an intrinsic nature,
then this intrinsic nature of wholesome dharmas should be explained part by part.
If the intrinsic nature of wholesome dharmas arises from causes and conditions, [it cannot be an intrinsic nature].
If wholesome phenomena are of another nature, how can they be of one's own nature?
If even a slight portion of wholesome phenomena were not born from causes and conditions,
and if wholesome phenomena were thus [uncaused], there would be no basis for abiding in the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Neither non-dharma nor dharma, nor even worldly dharmas exist;
if things possessed intrinsic nature, they would be eternal, and what is eternal lacks causes and conditions.
Whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—all conditioned phenomena [are likewise].
If it were as you say, then [the self] would be eternal; you would thus incur this fault.
If someone were to say that names exist and that speech possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), you may challenge that person; but for me, speech and names are not real.
If this "name" is non-existent, then existence would also be non-existent;
if you say it exists or does not exist, your thesis incurs two faults.
If this "name" exists, then non-existence would also be existent.
If you say there is no [position] or that there is [a position], your dispute involves two faults.
As I have previously stated, all phenomena are empty;
since my fundamental tenet is thus, no fault can be found.
If there were a separate intrinsic nature that did not reside within phenomena, you would have reason to worry about me for stating this;
however, such a thing is not necessary to worry about.
If there were an intrinsic nature, it could be negated; if it were empty, the statement could be established.
If there were no essence and no emptiness, how could negation be established?
What is it that you negate?
That which you negate is itself empty.
If phenomena are empty yet there is negation, then in this way your argument fails.
Since I do not possess even the slightest thing, I therefore do not negate;
thus you are without reason, falsely and arbitrarily challenging me.
Your words and the nature of phenomena are distinct; I shall now explain this meaning:
since no phenomenon can be expressed by speech, I am without fault.
You have cited the analogy of the mirage to clarify the great meaning.
Listen as I speak, employing appropriate similes:
If things possessed an intrinsic nature, they would not arise dependent on causes and conditions;
if they must depend on causes and conditions, then it can be said that they are empty.
If the self were to exist as a substantial reality, who could prevent or turn it back?
The same applies to other things; therefore, I am without fault.
As for this doctrine of causelessness, its meaning has already been fully explained above.
The cause is taught within the three times; it is taught as being equal.
If one teaches the cause within the three times, it is equal in the same way as before.
Thus, the cause within the three times is consistent with the teaching of emptiness.
If a person has faith in emptiness, that person has faith in all things;
if a person does not have faith in emptiness, they do not have faith in anything.
Emptiness is the nature of causes and conditions, taught as the Middle Way between the three [extremes] and the one.
"I take refuge and pay homage to that Supreme and Great Wisdom!
3. Explanation of the First Section of the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*. The third section of the explanation states:
At the beginning of the treatise, the verse says:
"If all things lack intrinsic nature,
and language itself lacks intrinsic nature, how can it negate that [intrinsic] nature?
What meaning does this verse clarify?

If all phenomena are entirely dependent on causes and conditions, then they are merely causes and conditions and the conjunction of causes and conditions; apart from these various causes and conditions, there is no further intrinsic nature whatsoever. Thus, all such phenomena are empty.

For example, the sprout does not exist within the seed; it does not exist within the conditions of earth, water, fire, wind, or space; it does not exist within each individual condition; it does not exist within the combination of all conditions; nor does it exist elsewhere apart from the conditions or their combination.
If all these things were entirely non-existent, one could say that the sprout lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If all things thus lacked intrinsic nature, they could be said to be empty. If all phenomena (*dharma*) were entirely empty, there would be no speech; and if there were no speech, it would be impossible to negate any phenomena.
If you think that while speech is not empty, all phenomena spoken by speech are empty, this meaning is not tenable. Why?
Because you say that all phenomena are empty, then speech itself must also be empty.
Why is this? Because it does not exist within the causes;

it does not exist within the four great elements, nor within each of them individually, nor within their combination, nor within the union or non-union of causes and conditions—in all these, it is entirely absent.

Such speech does not exist within the throat; it is absent in each of the lips, tongue, teeth, roots of the teeth, gums, nose, palate, and so forth. It is not present in their combination, nor is it present in both together; there is only the causal condition and the conjunction of causal conditions.
Apart from such a conjunction of causal conditions, there is no other distinct phenomenon.
If this is so, then all speech lacks intrinsic nature.
If speech thus lacks intrinsic nature, then all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
If these words lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then there would be only the name of negation, which could not negate phenomena.

For example, where there is no fire, there can be no burning; likewise, where there is no sword, there can be no cutting; and as there can be no waves where there is no water, so too, how could words that lack [intrinsic nature] negate the intrinsic nature of all phenomena?

Since it cannot negate the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena themselves, yet the mind recollects the negation of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, the meaning of "reversal" (*vṛtti*) is inconsistent.
Furthermore, there is another point, as the verse says:
"If speech has an intrinsic nature, The previously established thesis is destroyed."
"If this were so, there would be a fault; you ought to state a superior reason.
What does this verse clarify?
If these words possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the thesis (*siddhānta*) you previously established would be self-contradictory; thus, there would be a fault.
If that were so, you would have to provide a superior reason.
If your intention is that speech possesses intrinsic nature while other phenomena are empty, then this contradicts the emptiness of all phenomena, and your own thesis is likewise destroyed.
Furthermore, there is another meaning: speech is not separate from the enumeration of all phenomena;
if all phenomena are entirely empty, then speech is also empty.
If speech is empty, it cannot negate any phenomena.
If it is as you say, then among these six types [of arguments], there is a corresponding dispute; how then is that not inconsistent with your own position?
You assert that all phenomena are empty, and thus your words are also empty.
Why is this? Because speech itself is also among all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
If speech were empty, it would be unable to negate; if it were able to negate, then the statement that "all phenomena are empty" would be inconsistent.

Furthermore, if the corresponding speech were able to negate the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, then the speech that all phenomena are empty would itself not be empty; if it were not empty, its negation of all phenomena would be inconsistent.
If all phenomena are empty while language is not empty, what could that language possibly negate?
Furthermore, if this language were included within "all things," the analogy would be inconsistent.
If that language were itself part of "all things," then since all things are empty, language would also be empty; and if language is empty, it cannot negate anything.

If it is said that language is empty and all phenomena are also empty, and that emptiness can negate all phenomena to render them empty, then emptiness itself would be a causal condition; this, however, is untenable.
Furthermore, if you fear that the analogy is inappropriate,
[you might argue that] while the emptiness of all phenomena can act as a causal condition, such empty words cannot negate the intrinsic nature of all things.
Furthermore, there is another meaning: one side contains a fault because dharmas are both empty and not empty.
If that [position] contains a fault, we shall further state a superior reason.
If one side were empty and the other side were not empty, then to say that all phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic nature would be inconsistent with the meaning.
Furthermore, there is another point, as the verse says:
"If you claim it is like the sound 'do not,' that meaning is not so."
"If sound has the capacity to negate sound, how can the absence of sound negate it?
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?
If you think that sound can negate sound—just as someone might say, "Do not make a sound," and while making the sound themselves, they are able to negate it—[that is not so].
In this way, all phenomena are empty; thus, an empty statement can negate them.
This which I am now stating is inconsistent. Why is that?
Because this sound exists, it is able to negate that [other] sound;
however, since your statement does not exist, it cannot negate the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
According to your established position, both the statement and all phenomena are non-existent. Thus, if you claim it is like the word "do not," this entails a logical fallacy.
The verse says:
"Your claim that there is a negation and an object to be negated is likewise not so;
such a characteristic of your own thesis, being self-contradictory, does not belong to me."
What does this verse clarify?
If you intend that the negation and the object to be negated are likewise [mutually dependent], that is inconsistent.
If you say, "My statement can negate all phenomena while they possess intrinsic nature," that is inconsistent.
I shall now state this: that interpretation is incorrect.
Why? Because you have misunderstood the characteristics of this thesis; the fault lies with you, not with me.
You assert that all phenomena are empty; thus, according to your own position, your previous thesis contains a fault, and the blame does not lie with me.
If you say that your negation and the object to be negated are incompatible, this is not the case.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as the verse says:
"If that manifestation were existent, You could turn it away;
But since that manifestation is also non-existent, How can you take it up and turn it away?"
What does this verse clarify?
If all phenomena were such that they could be apprehended as manifest, you might succeed in turning my position so that all phenomena are empty; however, in reality, this is not the case.
How is this known?
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is included within the enumeration of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), and thus it too is empty.
If you distinguish that there is inference (*anumāna*) based on what exists through direct perception;
Perception and inference are both empty; since perception and inference do not exist in this way, how could perception and inference be apprehended?
Both of these being non-existent, how can they be negated?
As for your statement that all dharmas are empty, this meaning is not so.
If you further claim that all dharmas are apprehended through inference, analogy, or the *āgama*, [that too is incorrect].
Regarding the fact that I am able to turn back the intrinsic nature of all these phenomena—
this point is now explained.
The verse says:
"The four means of valid cognition—direct perception, inference, scripture, and analogy—are taught;
direct perception, inference, and scripture establish [the object], and analogy is also capable of establishing it.
What meaning does this verse clarify?

Regarding the four means of valid cognition—namely, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), scripture (*āgama*), and analogy (*upamāna*)—if direct perception can establish [an object], then inference, scripture, and the others can all likewise establish it.

Just as all phenomena are entirely empty, so too is direct perception empty; likewise, inference and analogy are also empty. All phenomena established by those means of valid cognition are entirely empty.

Because the four means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are present in all things, whatever dharma is established through inference is likewise established through analogy and established through scripture (āgama).

All phenomena established by him are entirely empty; you [employ] the three means of valid cognition—namely inference, analogy, and scripture (*āgama*)—to [establish] all phenomena, yet that which is measured by them is likewise empty.
If it were thus, dharmas could not be apprehended, and there would be neither the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor the object of cognition (*prameya*); therefore, there would be no negation.
Thus, if one says that all dharmas are empty and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the meaning [of such a statement] is inconsistent.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as the verse says:
"The wise person knows that when the Dharma is taught, The wholesome dharmas possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
Just as worldly people know that things have substance, So it is with all other dharmas."
What does this verse clarify?
The Dharma Master explains the wholesome dharmas; there are one hundred and nineteen wholesome dharmas, namely:
first, feeling (*vedanā*); second, perception (*saṃjñā*); third, volition (*cetanā*); fourth, contact (*sparśa*); fifth, investigation (*vitarka*).

74. Shame; 75. Integrity; 76. Non-deception; 77. Tranquility;
