97. Not possessing all-knowledge (asarvajña); 98. Absence of... [text fragment].
The *Samādhi of Constancy* lacks thirteen dharmas, and there is no place to seek their origin.
Such and such are the one hundred and nineteen wholesome dharmas.

Just as those wholesome dharmas have the intrinsic nature of wholesome dharmas, and those unwholesome dharmas have the intrinsic nature of unwholesome dharmas; likewise, the indeterminate and the indeterminate, the natural indeterminate and the natural indeterminate, the desire realm and the desire realm, the form realm and the form realm, the formless realm and the formless realm, the untainted and the untainted, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, and the cultivation of concentration and the cultivation of concentration—just so, one perceives that there are immeasurable varieties of all dharmas, each possessing its own intrinsic nature.
If it is thus asserted that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, and that this absence of nature constitutes emptiness, the meaning is inconsistent.
Furthermore, there is another point, as the verse says:
“The emergence of phenomena and the nature of the emergence of phenomena—this is what the Noble Ones have taught.”
"In this way, that which is non-emergent is the very nature of the non-emergent.
What does this verse clarify?
Just as that which emerges is the very nature of the emergent, so too that which is non-emergent is the very nature of the non-emergent.

The factors of enlightenment have the nature of the factors of enlightenment; the factors of awakening have the nature of the factors of awakening; and those that are not factors of awakening have the nature of not being factors of awakening. All other phenomena are likewise thus.

If one perceives those various infinite kinds of intrinsic natures of phenomena and yet asserts that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, claiming that the absence of intrinsic nature constitutes emptiness, this meaning is inconsistent.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as the verse says:
"If all phenomena have no intrinsic nature, That which lacks intrinsic nature cannot be named.
If there were an intrinsic nature, there would be a name; But how can that which is merely a name be called a 'name'?"
What does this verse clarify?
If all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then even the speech that asserts their lack of intrinsic nature would likewise be non-existent. Why is this so?
Where there is an entity, there is a name; where there is no entity, there is no name.

Since all phenomena possess names, one should know that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because phenomena possess intrinsic nature, it cannot be said that all phenomena are empty.
Thus, if one says that all phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic nature, the meaning is inconsistent.
As the verse says:
"If there were a name apart from phenomena, That [name] would not exist within those phenomena."
"If one says that names exist apart from dharmas, then that person may be challenged.
What meaning does this verse clarify?

If you intend to say that names exist because there are dharmas, or that names exist even apart from dharmas—in either case, it is established that all such dharmas are empty and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is not the case that there are no objects and yet names exist, nor that names exist only when there are objects.
This I shall now explain.
If it were as you say, what kind of person would claim that names exist separately from the essence of phenomena?
If name and phenomenon were separate entities, they could not be demonstrated [as such].
That cannot be demonstrated. Thus, your mind’s conceptualization that there are distinct phenomena and distinct names is incorrect.
Furthermore, there is another point, as the verse says:
“If phenomena possessed an intrinsic nature, One could negate those phenomena.”
If all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, what exactly is there to be negated?
Just as when there is a jar or clay, one can negate the jar or the clay;
seeing that something exists, one negates it, but seeing that nothing exists, one does not negate it.
What does this verse clarify?

An existent thing can be negated, whereas a non-existent thing cannot be negated. For example, if there is no jar or clay, there is no need for negation; however, when a jar exists, it can be negated, and when a jar is absent, it cannot be negated.
In this way, if phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is no need for negation; negation is possible only if phenomena possess an intrinsic nature that can be apprehended.

Since they lack it, how could there be negation? If all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, yet you proceed to negate them by saying, "All phenomena lack intrinsic nature," this is logically inconsistent: what is there for you to negate?
If there were a negating entity capable of negating the intrinsic nature of all phenomena,
the verse says:
"If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, what could language possibly negate?"
"If there is no dharma to be negated, even the absence of speech constitutes a negation.
What does this verse clarify?
If both the dharma and the speech lack intrinsic nature, how can there be negation?
If you say that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature,
then by such a negation, even the act of speaking words would constitute a negation;
if that were the case, there would be faults such as fire being cold or water being hard.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as the verse says:
"Just as a foolish person Mistakenly perceives a mirage as water,
If you were to negate that mistaken perception, The case would be exactly like this."
What does this verse clarify?
It means that if you think it is like a foolish person who perceives a mirage as water, falsely taking water where there is no water.
A wise person, in order to turn that mind away, says to them:
"You have falsely grasped at water.

In this same way, because sentient beings grasp at the intrinsic nature of phenomena within all phenomena that lack intrinsic nature, [the Buddha] teaches that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature in order to turn away their deluded minds.
I shall now explain this.
The verse says:
"Grasping, the grasped, and the grasper; The negated, the negation, and the negator."
"These six kinds of meanings are all existent phenomena.
What does this verse clarify?

If there were such a thing as a sentient being, then there would be the grasped and the object of grasping, as well as the grasper; thus one could speak of the false, the negation, and that which is negated, and these six kinds of meanings would be established.
If it were established by these six points that all phenomena are entirely empty, this meaning would not be correct.
As the verse says:
"If there is neither the grasped nor the object of grasping, There is likewise no grasper."
"Then there would be neither the object to be negated nor the act of negation, nor even one who negates.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
If you think that such a fault does not apply because [the self] is neither the grasped, the object of grasping, nor the grasper;

If one were to falsely grasp in such a manner that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, then that negation would not exist, the object negated would not exist, and the agent of negation would not exist either.
The verse says:
"If there were neither the negation nor the object of negation, nor even the agent of negation,
then all phenomena would be established, and their intrinsic nature would likewise be established."
What does this verse clarify?
If there is no negation, no object of negation, and no agent of negation, then nothing at all would be negated, and consequently, all phenomena would possess intrinsic nature.
The verse says:
"Your cause is not established; how can that which lacks intrinsic nature be a cause?
If a phenomenon has no cause, how can it be said to be established?"
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?
If all phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then within such a doctrine, the logical reason (*hetu*) is unestablished. Why is this so?
All phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic nature; where, then, could a cause exist?
If phenomena have no cause, by what cause would the emptiness of all phenomena be established?
Therefore, your assertion that all phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic nature is not tenable.
The verse says:
"If you establish [your position] without a cause, then the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is overturned;
yet I too establish [my position] without a cause, [namely] that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature."
What does this verse clarify?
If you intend to say that the self is established without a cause because phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
then just as your own self-nature is turned back upon itself as being established without a cause, so too my own-natured phenomena are established without a cause.
The verse says:
"If there were a cause that lacked an essence, this meaning would be inconsistent;
for in the world, a phenomenon that lacks an essence cannot be said to exist."
What does this verse clarify?
If you intend to say that "I" exist as established by causes, yet those causes lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
then if that were the case, the meaning of lacking intrinsic nature would be inconsistent.
Why is this? Because that which lacks intrinsic nature in all the world cannot be said to exist.
As the verse says:
"The prior negation and the subsequent object of negation—such being the case, they are not compatible.
If the subsequent negation and the [object] occur simultaneously, then one knows that there is an intrinsic nature.
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?
If the negation comes first and that which is to be negated comes later, the meaning is inconsistent.
If that which is to be negated does not yet exist, what is there for the negation to negate?
If the negation comes later and that which is to be negated comes earlier, this too is inconsistent.
Since that which is to be negated has already been established, how can the negation negate it?

If the negation and the object to be negated were simultaneous and not mutually dependent, then the negation would not depend on the object to be negated, nor would the object to be negated depend on the negation; because both would possess independent intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), one could not speak of "negation."
Just as when two horns grow simultaneously, each does not depend on the other— the left does not depend on the right, and the right does not depend on the left— so too,
if one says that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this meaning is not tenable.
The first part of the commentary is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Second Part of the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*, Part Four. The commentary states:
Regarding what you have said, I shall now answer you.
You have spoken this verse:
"If all things lack intrinsic nature, then speech itself is among those things;
since speech lacks intrinsic nature, how can it negate the intrinsic nature of others?"
I now respond to this verse with the following:
"If my words were separate from the phenomena produced by the harmony of causes and conditions,
then the meaning of emptiness would be established, and all dharmas would lack intrinsic nature."
What does this verse clarify?

If that speech does not exist within the causes, within the primary elements, or within their combination, nor does it exist when they are separated, and although the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, roots, gums, nose, and palate each possess their respective powers, yet [speech] does not exist within any one of these individual parts nor within their combination.
Apart from such a combination of causes and conditions, there is no other distinct phenomenon; because it is thus, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since it lacks intrinsic nature, my statement that "all things lack intrinsic nature" establishes the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Just as these words are empty of intrinsic nature, so too are all phenomena empty of intrinsic nature.
Therefore, your claim that "because your words are empty, they cannot express emptiness" is incorrect.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as the verse says:
"If the phenomena of causes and conditions are empty, I now explain this meaning:
what person possesses causes and conditions?"
"The causes and conditions of that have no essence.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
You are unable to understand the emptiness of all phenomena; not knowing the meaning of emptiness, how can you reproach me?
As you have said, your words are empty and lack intrinsic nature; because they lack intrinsic nature, they cannot negate phenomena.
If these phenomena are produced through causes and conditions, then by virtue of being produced, one can say that all phenomena are empty and that all things lack intrinsic nature.
For what reason is it known that phenomena produced through causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature?
If all phenomena are produced through causes and conditions, then all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they must depend upon causes and conditions; if they possessed intrinsic nature, what need would there be for causes and conditions?

If one is separated from causes and conditions, no phenomena exist; if they arise through causes and conditions, they possess no intrinsic nature. Because they lack intrinsic nature, they can be said to be empty.

In this way, my words also arise from causes and conditions; if they arise from causes and conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and because they lack intrinsic nature, they can be said to be empty.

Since all phenomena that arise from causes and conditions are empty of intrinsic nature—just as with objects such as carts, jars, garments, and blankets—each of those phenomena has its own respective causes and conditions.

The firewood and grass, earthen vessels, water, honey, milk, and so forth in the world—whether being brought or carried away, or held in the palm of the hand—as well as all objects of enjoyment within the hindrances of cold, heat, and wind, are all devoid of intrinsic nature because they arise from causes and conditions.
In this way, my statement arises through the combination of causes and conditions; thus, it can be said that it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If there is no intrinsic nature, then it can be said that the absence of intrinsic nature is established.

Since such empty speech is utilized by the world, your claim that "because [things] lack intrinsic nature, your words are also empty and thus cannot negate the intrinsic nature of phenomena" is incorrect.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as the verse says:

"Just as a conjured person acts toward a conjured person, and an illusory person acts toward an illusory person, so too is the negation of that which is to be negated; the meaning of this is likewise."
What does this verse clarify?
It is like a conjured man who, seeing another conjured man coming and going and performing various actions, proceeds to negate them;
or like an illusory man who, seeing another illusory man coming and going and performing various actions, proceeds to negate them.
That which can negate an illusory person is itself empty;
if that negating agent is empty, then the illusory person being negated is also empty.
If the object being negated is empty and the negating agent is also empty, then the illusory person who performs the negation is likewise empty.
If that person who negates is empty because they are like an illusory person, then the illusory person being negated is likewise empty.
If that which is negated is empty, then the person who negates is also empty.
In this way, my words are empty and like an illusion; such empty words are able to negate the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Therefore, your statement that "because your words are empty, they cannot negate the intrinsic nature of all phenomena" is inconsistent with your own position.
If you say that those six kinds of disputes are thus refuted, then in this way my statement is not among all phenomena.
My statement is empty and all phenomena are empty; it is not the case that all phenomena are entirely non-empty.
Furthermore, you have stated in verse:
"If speech possesses an intrinsic nature, The previously established thesis is undermined;
In that case, there is a fault, And one must further state a superior reason."
I now respond to this verse with the following:
"Speech has no intrinsic nature, and that which is spoken likewise lacks intrinsic nature.
Since I am thus without fault, there is no need to state a superior reason."
What does this verse clarify?
These words of mine arise through causes and conditions and do not possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
As previously stated, because an intrinsic nature is unarisen, it can be said to be empty; likewise, these words can be said to be empty, and all other phenomena are entirely empty as well.
Since it is empty in this way, I am without fault.
If I were to say that this statement is not empty while all other phenomena are entirely empty, then I would be at fault.
I am not like this; therefore, there is no fault.
In reality, it is not that language alone is non-empty while all other dharmas are entirely empty. For this reason, I do not state a superior cause.
If your speech were not empty while all other phenomena were entirely empty, one could speak of a superior reason [for its superiority].
Therefore, your statement that "your own argument fails and your speech is at fault, so you ought to state a superior reason" [is untenable].
This interpretation is not correct.
Furthermore, you have stated in verse:
"If one says it is like 'Do not make a sound,' this meaning is not so."
"If there is sound that can obstruct sound, how can the absence of sound obstruct it?
To this verse, I now reply with these verses:
"As for your mention of the word 'do not,' this is not a valid analogy for my case."
"Because this sound of mine cannot obstruct that other sound.
What does this verse clarify?
This is not my analogy.
As for those who say, "Do not make a sound," do they themselves produce a sound in order to use that sound to negate sound?
Sound is not non-empty.
I, however, am not like this; both speech and the negation are empty.
Why is this? For example, just as one sound can cause another sound to cease, I do not speak in such a manner.
I teach that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are said to be empty.

Why is this? If a statement lacking intrinsic nature were to negate the absence of intrinsic nature, then all phenomena would become established as having intrinsic nature—just as when one says the word "do not," that sound is able to obstruct another sound.

In this way, the statement that "there is no intrinsic nature" negates the dharma of non-existence; if one were thus to negate intrinsic nature, then all dharmas would become possessed of intrinsic nature, and if they possessed intrinsic nature, then all dharmas would not be empty.
I teach that phenomena are empty, not that they are non-empty; such is the analogy.
As the verse says:
"Just as some man might Falsely grasp at the body of a conjured woman..."
"And gives rise to a mind of desire—this meaning is also like this.
What does this verse clarify?

Just as a magically conjured woman is empty of any real intrinsic nature, if some man were to perceive that conjured female body as being truly existent and give rise to a mind of desire, that would be a false apprehension.
All phenomena are likewise.

Whether it be a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata—a śrāvaka—who, in order to turn back the mind of false grasping in such a person, or through the majestic spiritual power of a Tathāgata or the power of a disciple of the Tathāgata—a śrāvaka—manifests a transformation being (nirmāṇapuruṣa).
In this way, speech is empty like a magical creation; just as a magically created woman lacks intrinsic nature and is empty, so too are phenomena empty in this manner.
Grasping at the intrinsic nature of phenomena can obstruct and turn one back from this truth.
"In this way, and so forth, it is by means of this analogy of emptiness that the meaning of emptiness is established; thus, it accords with my position, not yours.
As the verse says:
"It is not the case that what is to be established is the same [as the example], because there is no cause within an echo."
"I speak thus based upon conventional truth.
What does this verse clarify?
If you should think that it is like the word "do not," then the reason is identical to the point to be proven.

Why is this? Because the cause does not exist apart from all phenomena which lack intrinsic nature; it is not that sound itself possesses an intrinsic nature, for since it arises through causes and conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature.
If there were no intrinsic nature, your claim that sound possesses the capacity to negate sound would be undermined.

Furthermore, what I teach does not contradict conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) nor does it abandon conventional truth; it is by relying upon conventional truth that one can declare the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
If one were to depart from conventional truth, phenomena could not be expressed.
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"If one does not rely on conventional truth, one cannot realize ultimate truth;
if one does not realize ultimate truth, one cannot attain the realization of nirvana."
What does this verse clarify?
It means that these phenomena are not non-empty; all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and these two [concepts] are no different.
Furthermore, you have spoken this verse:
"You claim that there is a negation and an object of negation; This is likewise not so.
If the characteristics of your own thesis thus destroy themselves, Then it is not mine."
I now respond to this verse with the following:
"If my school held that [things] exist, then I would indeed be at fault;
but since my school maintains that no entity exists, such a fault cannot be incurred."
What does this verse clarify?
If my school maintains that there is existence, then there must be the characteristics of a thesis (*pakṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
If I were to have a thesis and the characteristics of a thesis, I would incur the fault you previously pointed out.
In this way, I have no thesis; because all phenomena are truly quiescent and their intrinsic nature is empty, where could a thesis exist?
Regarding such characteristics of a thesis, in what place could the characteristics of a thesis be found?
I have no thesis-position (pakṣa) or characteristic marks (lakṣaṇa);
how can you find fault with me? Therefore, your statement that "you possess a thesis-position and thus incur a fault" is incorrect in meaning.
Furthermore, you have spoken this verse:
"If that manifestation were existent, You could turn it away;
But since that manifestation is also non-existent, How can it be turned away?"
"It is said that there are four means of valid cognition— direct perception, inference, scripture, and analogy—
and that these are established by direct perception, inference, and scripture, and that analogy can also establish them.
To this verse, I now reply with the following verse:
"If I were to grasp [the object] through a process of turning back, then one would have to employ [cognitions such as] the present and so forth.
There is a fault in grasping through a process of turning back; if it were not so, what fault would there be?
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?

If I were to possess even the slightest dharma or entity, it would have to be established by these four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), scripture (*āgama*), and analogy (*upamāna*).
Furthermore, there are four other [means]; if I were to adopt and employ them in such a manner, I would then be at fault.
Since I do not grasp even the slightest phenomenon to turn back from, if you were to charge me with a fault for thus neither turning nor returning, that argument would be untenable.
If a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were established by another means of valid cognition of equal measure, then there would be an infinite regress of means of valid cognition.
Your argument in this manner cannot refute me.
Furthermore, there is another point, as stated in the verse:
"If a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishes a phenomenon, and that [means of valid cognition] is itself established by another means of valid cognition, then tell me:
by what means of valid cognition can this [original] means of valid cognition be established?
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?

If you think that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishes objects—just as there are objects of valid cognition (*prameya*)—then by what further valid cognition are these four types of valid cognition, namely direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), scripture (*āgama*), and analogy (*upamāna*), established?
If these four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were established by further means of valid cognition, then the means of valid cognition themselves would not be established.
If those that are not themselves established could establish objects, then your own thesis would be undermined.
If the means of valid cognition were to be established by yet another distinct means of valid cognition, then there would be an infinite regress.
If there were no end, then it would not be established in the beginning, nor would it be established in the middle or at the end.

Why is this? If a means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) could establish the object of cognition (*prameya*), then that means of cognition itself would require another distinct means of cognition to establish it; [and so on ad infinitum].
Since that measure is established by another measure, there is thus no beginning;
if there is no beginning, there is likewise no middle;
and if there is no middle, where could there be an end?
Thus, if it is claimed that those means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are established by further distinct means of valid cognition, this argument is untenable.
As the verse says:
"If the means of valid cognition were established apart from the means of valid cognition, then your own position would be lost."
"If this were so, there would be a fault; you ought to state a superior reason.
What does this verse clarify?

If your intention is that the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established independently of other means of cognition, while the objects of cognition (*prameya*) are established by those means of cognition—if you argue in this manner that the means of cognition establish the objects of cognition, then you fall into error.
There are things established through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and those not so established; if this is the case, one should state the superior reason (*viśeṣahetu*).
If the superior reason is stated, then it can be known which [things] are established by valid cognition and which are not.
You are unable to demonstrate such a distinction; your argument is inconsistent with the meaning.
This I shall now explain.
Suppose someone were to say, "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that I have described establishes both itself and others," and then spoke this verse:
"Just as because fire is luminous, it can illuminate both itself and others, so too is that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); both itself and others are established.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
Just as fire illuminates itself and can also illuminate others, so too is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): it establishes both itself and others.
Now, I answer him with this verse:
"Your statement contains a fallacy; it is not that fire illuminates itself."
"Because that [inference] is inconsistent, it is like seeing a jar in the dark.
What does this verse clarify?
That objection—that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), like fire, can establish both itself and others—is inconsistent.
Why is this? Fire does not illuminate itself.
Just as at first it has not yet illuminated and jars and other objects in the darkness cannot be seen, once the fire has illuminated them, they can then be seen.
In this way, if fire were to illuminate itself, the initial fire would have to be dark and only later become bright; only then could it be said that fire is able to illuminate itself.
If the initial fire is already bright, then it cannot be said that fire is able to illuminate itself.
Thus, the analysis that fire illuminates both itself and others is logically inconsistent.
Furthermore, there is another point, as the verse says:
"Moreover, if you say that fire can illuminate both itself and others,"
"If fire can burn others, why does it not burn itself?
What meaning does this verse clarify?
If you say that just as fire illuminates itself and also illuminates others, so too does it illuminate itself and illuminate others.
In this way, if it were truly so, that which can burn another should also burn itself; yet, in reality, such a thing is not observed.
Therefore, the claim that fire illuminates both itself and others is logically inconsistent.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as the verse says:
"If you further claim that fire can illuminate both itself and others,
then darkness should likewise [be able to] cover both itself and others."
What does this verse clarify?
If you say that fire illuminates both itself and others and is thus able to dispel darkness, why does darkness not likewise cover both itself and others?
In reality, however, no such thing is observed.
If it were said that fire illuminates both itself and others, this meaning would be inconsistent.
Furthermore, there is another point, as the verse says:
"In fire there is no darkness; where could self or other abide?
Since that darkness can destroy light, how could fire possess light?
What meaning does this verse clarify?
There is no darkness within fire, nor is there darkness where fire is present; how, then, can it be said that light is able to destroy darkness?
If there is thus no darkness within that fire, where could there be darkness for the fire to destroy?
If there were no darkness to be destroyed, how could it illuminate both itself and others?
To this, I now respond:

If that were so, it would not be darkness within the fire, nor darkness in the place of the fire; in such a manner does the fire illuminate both itself and others, for at the very moment that fire arises, it is capable of destroying darkness.
Thus, there is no darkness within the fire, nor is there darkness where the fire is; in this way, the arising of fire is able to illuminate both itself and others.
This I shall now explain.
The verse says:
"When fire arises, it illuminates at the very moment of its arising;
yet for fire to reach darkness at that same moment is logically inconsistent.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
If fire, at the moment of its arising, were able to illuminate both itself and others, this would be logically inconsistent.
How is this known?
It is because such an initial fire cannot reach the darkness.
How is this known?
If light has not yet reached the darkness, it cannot destroy the darkness; and if it does not destroy the darkness, there can be no manifestation of light.
As the verse says:
"If fire could destroy darkness without reaching it,
then while staying right here, it should destroy all darkness.
What meaning does this verse clarify?

If you think that fire can destroy darkness without reaching it, then since fire remains in its own location, it should be able to destroy all the darkness existing in every location throughout the world.
Why is this? Because neither has arrived.
Yet, in reality, no such thing is observed.
If neither [fire nor darkness] reaches the other, why does it only destroy the darkness in this particular place and not the darkness in all places throughout the world?
If you intend to argue that fire can destroy darkness without reaching it, that reasoning is inconsistent.
Furthermore, there is another meaning expressed in the verse:
“If a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were to establish itself independently, Without depending on that which is to be cognized (*prameya*),
Then this means of valid cognition would be self-established, And not established by depending on something else.”
What does this verse clarify?

If you intend that the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*) are established like fire, then the means of cognition would be self-established, without depending on the object of cognition.
Why is this? If it were self-established, it would not depend on another; if it depends on another, it is not self-established.
This is what I shall now explain.
If it did not depend [on others], why would it not be self-established?
If it depends on another, then it is not self-established.
This is what I am now saying.
If valid cognition did not depend upon the object of cognition, what fault would there be?
I shall now explain this.
The verse says:
"If your means of cognition were established without depending on the object to be cognized,
then there would be no person who employs a means of cognition to cognize all phenomena.
What meaning does this verse clarify?

If you think that the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) can be established without depending on the object of cognition (*prameya*), then there would be the fault that no one would employ a means of cognition to cognize an object.
If anyone at all required a means of cognition, they could possess such a means of cognition without depending on an object of cognition.
If they do not depend on establishment, what fault would that entail?
It would mean that all phenomena do not depend on valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If all phenomena were established without depending on valid cognition, what fault would that entail?
That which is established can be said to be established, whereas that which is not yet established cannot be established, because it lacks dependence.

If you further claim that the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established by depending on the objects of cognition (*prameya*), then these four means of cognition would all be established through dependence.
Why is this? If an entity has not yet been produced, how can there be mutual dependence?
If an entity has already been produced, there is no need for mutual dependence.

That which has not yet been attained or accomplished does not depend on external objects; likewise, that which has already been accomplished does not need to be accomplished again, just as an object that has already been made requires no further causal conditions for its making.
Furthermore, there is another principle expressed in this verse:
"If the object of measurement Depends upon the means of measurement to be established,"
"This is what is established by the means of cognition; it is established only after depending upon the means of cognition.
What does this verse clarify?
If the object to be cognized (*prameya*) is established only by depending on the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is by means of that cognition that the object to be cognized is established.
Why is this? That which is established is not established; it is by means of the measure (*pramāṇa*) that the object of measurement (*prameya*) is established.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as the verse says:
"If an object were established without a means of cognition, it would not depend upon a means of cognition;
why then do you claim it is established by a means of cognition?
And what, then, would that means of cognition establish?"
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?

If you intend that the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*) are established without depending on one another, why do you now seek to establish them through a means of cognition?
For what reason?
For what purpose is that object of measurement sought?
If the object to be measured were established independently of the means of measurement, what would be the use of that measurement?
Furthermore, there is another point, as stated in the verse:
"If your means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) were established by depending on that which is to be cognized (*prameya*),
then the means of cognition and the object of cognition would be thus inseparable.
What is the meaning elucidated by this verse?
If you think that the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists because it depends upon the object of cognition (*prameya*), you fear falling into the aforementioned error.
If this were so for you, the means of cognition and the object of cognition would be one and could not be separated;
if this were so for you, the means of cognition would be identical to the object of cognition.
How is this known? That which is the object of cognition establishes the means of cognition; thus, the object of cognition is itself the means of cognition.
That which is the means of cognition establishes the object of cognition; thus, the means of cognition and the object of cognition are one.
The verse says:
"If the means of cognition establish the object of cognition, and if the object of cognition establishes the means of cognition,
then according to your view, neither of the two would be established."
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?

If you intend that the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishes the object of cognition (*prameya*) because it depends upon the object of cognition, and that the object of cognition establishes the means of cognition because it depends upon the means of cognition; [then...]
If it were as you say, both would be unestablished. Why?
As the verse says:
"If the means of cognition can establish the object of cognition,
and the object of cognition can establish the means of cognition— if this were the case, how could they establish one another?
What meaning does this verse clarify?

If the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) were to establish the object of cognition (*prameya*), and that object of cognition were in turn to establish the means of cognition, then since the means of cognition itself would not yet be established, its causal conditions would be unformed; how then could it establish the object of cognition?
Furthermore, there is another meaning expressed in the verse:
"The object of cognition establishes the means of cognition, And the means of cognition establishes the object of cognition.
If this were the case, How could they establish one another?"
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?

If the object of cognition (*prameya*) could establish that means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that means of cognition could establish the object of cognition, then since the object of cognition has not yet been established, its causal conditions would not be established; how, then, could the means of cognition be established?
The verse says:
"Does the father give birth to the son?
Or does the son give birth to the father?"
"What is that which gives rise [to something],
and what is that which is given rise to?
What meaning does this verse clarify?
Suppose someone were to say that the father can produce the son; if that were so, then the son would also produce the father.
You must now explain which of these two is the producer and which is the produced.

You have stated that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishes the object of valid cognition (*prameya*), and the object of valid cognition establishes the means of valid cognition; yet you have not now explained which of these is the establisher and which is the established.
Furthermore, there is another point, as the verse says:
"What constitutes a father?
What constitutes a son?
You have spoken of these two; the relationship between father and son is thus open to doubt."
What is the meaning elucidated by this verse?
Regarding the two types previously mentioned— namely, father and son—
who is the father and who is the son?
If the two characteristics of father and son arise in mutual dependence, then that is questionable: which is the father?
Which is the son? In this same way, if you speak of this means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*), which of them is the means of cognition?
What is the object of cognition?

Regarding these two types [of means and objects], if they can establish an entity, they may be called the "means of cognition" (pramāṇa); if the entity can be established, it may be called the "object of cognition" (prameya). Thus, there is no doubt as to what constitutes the means of cognition.
What is the object of cognition?

That which can be established in such a way may be called "cognition" (pramāṇa), and that which can be so established may be called the "object of cognition" (prameya). Thus, there is no doubt as to what constitutes cognition.
What is that which is measured?
The verse says:
"The means of cognition is not established by itself, nor is it established by both itself and another."
"It is not established by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), nor is it established without causes and conditions.
What does this verse clarify?

Such means of valid cognition are not self-established: perception is not established by perception, inference is not established by inference, analogy is not established by analogy, and "scripture" (āgama) is likewise not established by "scripture."

It is not that these are established through mutual dependence of self and other—such that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not established by inference (*anumāna*), analogy (*upamāna*), or scripture (*āgama*); inference is not established by direct perception, analogy, or scripture; analogy is not established by direct perception, inference, or scripture; and scripture is not established by direct perception, inference, or analogy.

Nor is it that there exist separate instances of direct perception, inference, analogy, and scripture distinct from [the categories themselves], nor that they are established by some other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) different from these.

In accordance with their measure, they are not established through the combination of internal parts; they are not established through the combination of internal and external spheres; they are not established without a cause, nor are they established through accumulation.
These causal conditions are as previously explained: twenty, thirty, or four, five, or six; twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or perhaps sixty.

If, as you have stated, it can be said that because there is a means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is an object of cognition (*prameya*), and that the existence of these means and objects of cognition proves that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this argument is inconsistent with reason.
Furthermore, you have spoken this verse:
"The wise person, knowing the Dharma as it is taught, Understands that wholesome dharmas possess intrinsic nature;
The people of the world know they possess such nature, And other dharmas are likewise so."
"The arising of phenomena arises from their own nature; this is what the Noble Ones have taught.
Likewise, the non-arising of phenomena [arises] from the own-nature of non-arising.
To this verse, I now reply with the following verse:
"If what the Dharma Master says is that wholesome dharmas possess an intrinsic nature,
then this intrinsic nature of wholesome dharmas ought to be explained part by part.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
If that Dharma-master maintains that those wholesome phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), he should explain this wholesome intrinsic nature part by part.
This wholesome phenomenon would be like that wholesome mind and the intrinsic nature of that wholesome mind.
In this way, all phenomena are not to be viewed as such; if one were to speak thus, it would also be inconsistent with the meaning of the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Furthermore, there is another point, as the verse says:
"If the intrinsic nature of wholesome phenomena Arises from causes and conditions,"
If wholesome dharmas have another as their substance, how can they have a self-substance?
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?

If the substance of wholesome dharmas arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions, then that [conjunction] is another substance; how then could the wholesome dharmas possess a self-substance?
Just as it is with the intrinsic nature of wholesome phenomena, so it is with the others.

If you say that just as those wholesome phenomena have the intrinsic nature of being wholesome, so too do unwholesome phenomena have the intrinsic nature of being unwholesome, this meaning is inconsistent.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as the verse says:
"If even a slight wholesome dharma Were not produced from causes and conditions,
If wholesome dharmas were thus, There would be no abiding in the holy life."
What does this verse clarify?

If you intend to say that there exists even a slight wholesome dharma that is not produced by causes and conditions— such as unwholesome dharmas having an unwholesome intrinsic nature, or indeterminate dharmas having an indeterminate intrinsic nature—
if it were so, there would be no abiding in the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Why is this? If you act in such a manner, you will abandon the twelve links of dependent origination;
if you abandon the twelve links of dependent origination, you will thereby abandon the vision of the twelve links of dependent origination.
If, in this way, the twelve links of dependent origination do not exist, then one cannot perceive the twelve links of dependent origination;
and if one does not perceive the twelve links of dependent origination, one cannot perceive the Dharma.
The Blessed One said:
"If a bhikṣu sees the twelve links of dependent origination, he sees the Dharma.
If he does not see the Dharma, he does not abide in the holy life."
If one is free from these twelve links of dependent origination, then one is free from the origin of suffering, for the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the origin of suffering;
if one is free from the origin of suffering, then one is free from suffering, for if there is no origin, where could suffering exist?
If there were no suffering, how could there be its cessation?
If there were no cessation of suffering, where would one cultivate the path to the cessation of suffering?

If this were the case, the Four Noble Truths would not exist; and if the Four Noble Truths do not exist, then the fruits of the śrāvaka path would likewise not exist—for it is by seeing the Four Noble Truths that one realizes the fruits of the śrāvaka path. Without the fruits of the śrāvaka, there would be no abiding in the holy life (brahmacarya).
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as the verse says:
“Neither dharma nor non-dharma, Nor even worldly dharmas exist.
If there were an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it would be eternal; And that which is eternal is without causes and conditions.”
What does this verse clarify?

If things were to arise in such a way—detached from the conjunction of causes and conditions—you would incur many faults; for since neither dharma nor adharma could be apprehended, all worldly phenomena would be unattainable.
Why is this? All phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, for all phenomena are produced through the conjunction of causes and conditions;
if they were not produced through the conjunction of causes and conditions, then no phenomena whatsoever could be apprehended.
Furthermore, its own essence does not arise from the combination of causes and conditions; if it existed without causes and conditions, it would be a permanent phenomenon.
Why is this? Because a phenomenon that lacks causes and conditions is permanent.
If it were as you say, there would be no abiding in the holy life (brahmacarya).
Furthermore, your own doctrine contains an internal inconsistency. Why is this?
The Blessed One has taught that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are entirely impermanent.
What is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) such that they are all impermanent?
The verse says:
"Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—all conditioned phenomena would, according to what you say, be eternal; thus you fall into such an error.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
If you say that wholesome phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and you say the same for unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena—
if this is so, then you are asserting that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are eternal.
Why is this? If phenomena were without cause, they would lack arising, abiding, and ceasing.
If they lacked arising, abiding, and ceasing, they would not be conditioned phenomena; consequently, all phenomena would be unconditioned.
If you claim that all phenomena, such as the wholesome and so forth, possess an intrinsic nature, then it follows that all phenomena are not empty; this meaning is inconsistent with reason.
Furthermore, you have stated in verse:
"If all phenomena lack an intrinsic nature, then that which lacks an intrinsic nature cannot be named."
"If there is a name for an intrinsic nature, how can that which is merely a name be called a 'name'?
To this verse I now reply with these verses:
"If one says that names exist, then speech would possess an intrinsic nature."
"You may challenge that person who says, 'The designation "I" is not real.
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?
If anyone asserts that the designation has an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), you may then challenge that person in such a manner.
That person says that where there is substance there is a name, and where there is no substance there is no name.
I do not speak in this way regarding the existence of names and substances.
How is this known?
All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; if they lack intrinsic nature, they can be said to be empty. If they are empty, they can be said to be unreal.
If you maintain that names possess intrinsic nature, this meaning is inconsistent.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as the verse says:
"If this name does not exist, Then existence would also be non-existent.
If you speak of both existence and non-existence, Your own thesis incurs two faults."
"If this 'existence' exists, then 'non-existence' would also exist;
if you claim both non-existence and existence, your dispute contains two fallacies.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
If this name does not exist, then our thesis is lost;
if it does exist, then the dispute is lost. Our thesis is not like that.
Where there is a thing, there is a name; where there is no thing, there is no name.
Thus, the notion that these phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is logically inconsistent.
Furthermore, there is another point, as stated in the verse:
"As I have previously stated, all phenomena are empty;
such is the tenet of my doctrine, and thus no fault can be found.
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?
I have already stated previously that all phenomena are empty, and that "emptiness" is also designated as a name.
You grasp at the name "emptiness" and then offer your critique.

If all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, then names likewise lack intrinsic nature; my statement is thus free from error in its fundamental tenet, for I do not assert that names possess intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, you have spoken this verse:
"If there were a name apart from dharmas, Not existing within the dharmas themselves,
To say that there is a name apart from dharmas— Such a person may indeed be challenged."
I now respond to this verse with the following:
"If there were a separate intrinsic nature That did not reside within phenomena, Then your concern for me in stating this Would indeed be necessary; but it is not so."
What does this verse clarify?
It means that you need not worry about my being falsely accused; I do not negate the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena, nor do I apprehend any entity as existing apart from those phenomena.
Whoever grasps at dharmas must be concerned;
since I do not grasp at dharmas, I do not obstruct them—how, then, could there be any fault?
If I were to grasp at dharmas as having intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then you might rightly challenge me by saying that my position is inconsistent.
I do not hold such a view; your objection is far-fetched and entirely irrelevant.
Furthermore, you have stated in verse:
"If dharmas possessed an intrinsic nature, One could negate those dharmas."
Since all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, what exactly is being negated?
Just as when there is a jar and there is clay, one can negate the jar or the clay;
one negates upon seeing an existing thing, but does not negate when seeing a non-existent thing.
I now respond to this verse with the following:
"If there were an entity, negation could be established; If there were emptiness, affirmation could be established.
But if there is neither entity nor emptiness, How can negation or affirmation be established?"
What does this verse clarify?
If a phenomenon exists, then that phenomenon can be negated; if it does not exist, it cannot be negated.
You challenge me by saying that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; indeed, it is as you say—that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
How is this known?
It is because by negating you, the absence of intrinsic nature in phenomena is established.
If the negation of the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena is established, one may say that all phenomena are empty.
The verse says:
"What is it that you negate?
That which you negate is empty."
“If phenomena are empty yet there is negation, such is your defeat in debate.
What does this verse clarify?
If all phenomena were negated while possessing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then only that which lacks intrinsic nature could be called empty; yet even that emptiness would itself be empty.
Therefore, your statement that "an existent thing can be negated, while a non-existent thing cannot be negated" is logically inconsistent.
Furthermore, there is another point, as the verse says:
"I do not possess even the slightest thing; therefore, I do not negate anything."
"In this way, you have no reason, yet you have unjustly challenged me.
What does this verse clarify?
If I were obstructed by even the slightest thing in such a manner, you would be entitled to challenge me.
I have no entity to obstruct; likewise, since there is no entity, I have nothing to obstruct. Thus, because there is no obstruction, all phenomena are empty.
Since there is thus no entity that obstructs nor anything to be obstructed, your previous objection—asking "What is it that is obstructed?"—is an unreasonable and baseless attempt to misrepresent me.
Furthermore, you have stated in verse:
"If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, what is there for speech to negate?
If a phenomenon could be negated by speech, then even in the absence of speech, negation would be established."
I now respond to this verse with the following:
"The words you speak and the phenomena [they describe] are distinct; I shall now explain this meaning.
Since no phenomenon can be expressed by speech, I am without fault."
What does this verse clarify?

If you say that even the absence of words constitutes a negation, then according to that principle, all phenomena whatsoever lack intrinsic nature; it is the statement "all phenomena lack intrinsic nature" that expresses this, not these very words themselves that lack intrinsic nature.
To this I now reply: if one speaks the words "all phenomena lack intrinsic nature," these words do not themselves produce phenomena that lack intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, there is another meaning:
by means of the absence of a phenomenal essence, one knows the absence of a phenomenal essence; and by means of the presence of a phenomenal essence, one knows the presence of a phenomenal essence.

For example, suppose there is truly no Devadatta in a house. If someone asks, "Is there a Devadatta in this house? and one person answers, "There is," while another answers, "There is not," the one who says there is not replies:
"One cannot create the absence of Devadatta within that house; one simply knows that the house is empty and devoid of Devadatta."

Thus, if one says that "all phenomena lack intrinsic nature," this statement does not bring about the non-existence of all phenomena as lacking intrinsic nature; rather, it simply makes known that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is itself without substance.

If you say, "If there were no entity, one could not say that phenomena lack intrinsic nature; because there would be no statement, it would be impossible to establish that phenomena lack intrinsic nature," this argument is inconsistent with reason.
Furthermore, you spoke this verse:
"Just as a foolish person falsely perceives a mirage as water,
if you were to negate that false perception, the matter would be exactly like that."
The grasped and the grasper, the negated and the negator—
these six categories of meaning are all existent phenomena.
If there were no grasped or object of grasping, there would likewise be no grasper.
Then there would be neither the negated nor the negation, nor would there be a negator.
If there were neither the negated nor the negation, nor a negator,
then all phenomena would be established, and their intrinsic nature would likewise be established.
Regarding these four lines of verse, I now answer you with these verses:
"You have spoken the parable of the mirage To clarify the great meaning;
listen as I provide my response In accordance with that very analogy."
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?
If you claim that this analogy of the mirage is intended to illustrate a great principle, then listen as I provide an answer consistent with that analogy.
The verse says:
"If that [entity] possessed an intrinsic nature, it would not need to arise from causes and conditions;
if it requires causes and conditions, then it may be said to be empty.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
If the illusory perception of water within a mirage were not produced by causes and conditions, then your analogy would be appropriate.

However, that perception of water arises from the causal conditions of the mirage; it is a distorted perception, and such a distorted perception arises because one does not investigate causes and conditions. Thus, it can be said that it is produced by causes and conditions.
If that intrinsic nature arises from causes and conditions, its emptiness is as explained previously.
Furthermore, there is another point expressed in this verse:
"If the intrinsic nature were real, Who could possibly obstruct or turn it back?"
"The rest are also like this; therefore, I am without fault.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
If the substance of water were truly present within the mirage of the "deer-thirst" (mṛgatṛṣṇā), who could ever turn it away?
If there were an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it could not be reversed—just as fire is hot, water is moist, and space is unobstructed.
Seeing that this can be reversed, one thus grasps that intrinsic nature is empty; in this same manner, the meaning regarding other phenomena should be understood accordingly.
Just as grasping is without reality, so it is with the other five [aggregates].
If you claim that those six phenomena exist and thus assert that "all phenomena are not empty," this meaning is inconsistent.
Furthermore, you have stated in verse:
“Your reason is not established; how can there be a reason for that which lacks intrinsic nature?
If a phenomenon has no cause, how can it be said to be established?”
If you establish [your position] without a reason, then the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is refuted;
likewise, I too establish [my position] without a reason, that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature.
If there were a reason but no intrinsic nature, this meaning would be inconsistent.
"If there were no dharmas without substance in the world, then one could not say they exist.
To this verse, I now reply with these verses:
"As for this teaching of causelessness, its meaning has already been fully explained above."
"The cause is taught throughout the three times; it is taught as being equal.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
Such a great significance has already been explained previously; one should understand that, in this case, there is no [independent] cause.
Regarding this point of argument, the previous reasons have already explained the refutation of the six types of reversal; that preceding argument is now stated here.
Furthermore, you have stated in verse:
"The prior negation and the subsequent object of negation— such a [relationship] is inconsistent."
"Later, if both [cause and effect] are simultaneously negated, one thus knows that they possess substantiality.
To this verse, I now reply with these verses:
"If one asserts causes in the three times, it is likewise equal to the former case."
"Thus, the causes of the three times are in accord with the teaching of emptiness.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
If one were to negate these causes through verbal expressions regarding the three times, this has already been answered previously; it should be understood in this way.
Why is this? Because of equality.
Just as the three times were refuted as being mutually incompatible, so too does that statement reside within both the negation and the object of negation.

If you think that negation still occurs even when there is no object to be negated, then since I have already completed the negation, these three temporal reasons are consistent with the speech of one who propounds emptiness.
Furthermore, how was this previously explained?
As stated in the verse above:
"I do not possess even the slightest thing; therefore, I do not negate."
"In this way, you are without reason, and you have unjustly challenged me.

If you further claim that [the effect] is established by negation across three times—seeing the cause at the prior time, seeing the cause at the subsequent time, and seeing the cause at the simultaneous time—then [it follows that...]
The prior cause is like a father with respect to his son; the subsequent cause is like a teacher with respect to his disciple; and the simultaneous cause is like a lamp with respect to its light.
This "self" which I now describe is not like these.
The three types previously mentioned each possess three further faults, which have already been explained above.
Furthermore, by sequentially refuting the faults in your established thesis (*siddhānta*), such [arguments] constitute a refutation of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) through its own terms.
The verse says:
"If a person has faith in emptiness, that person has faith in all things;
if a person does not have faith in emptiness, they do not have faith in anything."
What does this verse clarify?
If a person has faith in emptiness, that person then has faith in all mundane and supramundane phenomena. Why is this so?
If a person believes in emptiness, they believe that things arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions;
if they believe that things arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, they believe in the Four Noble Truths;
if they believe in the Four Noble Truths, that person believes in all supreme realizations.
If a person can have faith in all supreme realizations, they will then have faith in the Triple Gem—namely, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
If they believe that things arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, that person believes in the causes and effects of the Dharma;
if a person can believe in the causes and effects of the Dharma, that person will then believe in the causes and effects of what is not the Dharma.

If a person can believe in the cause of dharmas and the fruit of dharmas, and believe in the cause of non-dharmas and the fruit of non-dharmas, then they will believe in afflictions, the conjunction of afflictions, and the entities of the dharma of afflictions.
That person thus believes in all these things as previously described; such a person then believes in wholesome and unwholesome actions.
If a person can believe in wholesome and unwholesome actions, they then believe in the dharmas of wholesome and unwholesome conduct.
If a person can believe in the dharmas of wholesome and unwholesome conduct, they will know the skillful means to transcend the three evil realms.
That person is thus able to believe in all phenomena of the world; such [phenomena] are immeasurable and cannot be fully described.
"Emptiness as the intrinsic nature of causes and conditions—this is taught as the Middle Way of the three-in-one.
I take refuge in and pay homage to that Supreme, Great Wisdom!"
The explanation of the meaning of the verses of the *Vigrahavyāvartanī* is hereby completed.
(The author of this treatise is the Ācārya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nāgārjuna, who is capable of explaining all points of doctrinal argument.)
